slides.headline: Tradie? Your body is the main tool

slides.title: Site work is repetitive load
slides.body: Kneeling, lifting, reaching overhead and twisting in tight spaces, often for hours. Most tradie niggles come from doing a lot of the same thing without enough built-up capacity for it.

slides.title: Strength for awkward positions
slides.body: Gym machines train neat, stable movements. Pilates trains control through odd angles, like lifting from a twisted position or holding a half squat while you work under a sink.

slides.title: Hips and mid-back share the load
slides.body: When your hips and upper back move well, your lower back does less of the twisting. Rotation and hip mobility work are usually a big part of a tradie's program.

slides.title: Small sessions that fit the week
slides.body: One or two sessions a week plus ten minutes of home exercises is a realistic start. The home moves need no gear and can be done before you head to site.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Back pain with leg numbness or weakness, pain after a fall from a ladder or height, or a niggle that keeps building week after week is worth a proper assessment first.

topic: Christmas cooking marathon: back care in the kitchen

slides.headline: Cooking for twelve this Christmas?
slides.sub: Long hours at the bench add up. A few kitchen tweaks help.

slides.title: Bring the job up to you
slides.body: Benches suit some heights better than others. For long chopping jobs, a thick board raises the work, or sit at the table for peeling and prepping so your back gets a break.

slides.title: Stagger your stance
slides.body: Standing square to the bench for an hour loads the same tissues nonstop. Rest one foot on a low step or open cupboard shelf, and swap sides every few minutes.

slides.title: Lift the roast with a plan
slides.body: Heavy trays come out of low ovens. Squat down close, keep the tray near your body and turn with your feet, not your spine. Grab a helper for the big ones.

slides.title: Break the marathon into rounds
slides.body: Prep in 20 to 30 minute rounds. Between them, walk the hallway, do a few standing back bends or sit for a minute. Small breaks usually beat one long rest at the end.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Back pain that spreads down a leg, numbness, pain that wakes you and won't ease, or a sudden flare-up that isn't settling after a few days is worth an assessment.

topic: Rib pain after coughing or twisting

slides.headline: Sharp rib pain after a big cough?
slides.sub: Why ribs get sore, and how to stay comfortable while they settle.

slides.title: Ribs move with every breath
slides.body: Your ribs connect to your spine and breastbone through small joints and muscles between each rib. A hard cough, sneeze or awkward twist can strain them, and they often complain for a while.

slides.title: Why it catches on a deep breath
slides.body: Coughing, laughing and rolling over in bed all move the ribs. That's why pain can feel sharp on these movements yet ease when you're still. It's usually irritation, not harm.

slides.title: Keep breathing deeply
slides.body: Shallow breathing to avoid pain can leave you stiffer. A few slow, deep breaths each hour, and hugging a pillow when you cough, can make things more comfortable.

slides.title: Gentle movement helps
slides.body: Easy walking, slow side bends and gentle rotation within comfort usually help more than staying rigid. Many rib strains settle over a few weeks as you keep moving.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: See your GP promptly for chest pain with breathlessness, fever, coughing up blood, pain after a fall or knock, or pain that is severe or getting worse. Call 000 in an emergency.

topic: Hip flexor strain in kicking sports

slides.headline: Front of hip grabs when you kick?
slides.sub: A hip flexor strain is common in kicking sports. Here's the road back.

slides.title: Where it usually happens
slides.body: Kicking, sprinting and quick changes of direction load the hip flexors hard, especially when you're tired late in a game. Pain at the front of the hip or top of the thigh is typical.

slides.title: Keep moving, but adjust
slides.body: Complete rest usually slows things down. Walking, cycling or swimming within comfort keep you fit while the strain settles. Pain up to a mild, settling level is usually okay.

slides.title: Load it back up gradually
slides.body: Start with gentle holds like lifting your knee against your hand, then progress to marching, lunges and resisted knee drives. Strength before speed is a good rule.

slides.title: Kicking comes last
slides.body: Build from passing short to long, then shooting, then full-speed kicks. Most people move up a step when the previous one feels easy the next morning.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A pop with sudden pain, trouble walking, a lump or bruising, or groin pain that keeps coming back is worth an assessment rather than playing through it.

topic: Keeping up Pilates over the holidays: a 10-minute routine

slides.headline: Holidays? Keep 10 minutes for Pilates
slides.sub: A simple mat routine for a hotel room or a beach towel.

slides.title: Minutes 1 to 2: breathe and bridge
slides.body: Lie on your back, knees bent. Take five slow breaths into your ribs, then do ten bridges, rolling up and down one segment at a time. No rush, no gear needed.

slides.title: Minutes 3 to 4: dead bug
slides.body: Lie on your back with arms up and knees at 90 degrees. Slowly lower one arm and the opposite leg, then swap. Keep your lower back steady. Eight each side.

slides.title: Minutes 5 to 6: side-lying legs
slides.body: Lie on your side, hips stacked. Lift the top leg slowly, then do small circles. Ten lifts and five circles each way, then roll over and repeat on the other side.

slides.title: Minutes 7 to 8: bird dog
slides.body: On hands and knees, reach one arm forward and the opposite leg back. Pause, return and swap. Eight each side, moving slowly enough to keep your hips level.

slides.title: Minutes 9 to 10: open the spine
slides.body: Finish with cat-cow for ten slow rounds, then thread the needle for five each side. A good wind-down after a day of travel or a long lunch.

slides.headline: Pick up where you left off
slides.body: Our Pilates team can tweak your program for travel, then progress it when you're back. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:
Heading away for the holidays? Your Pilates doesn't have to go on hold. 🏖️

You don't need a reformer to keep your strength ticking over. Ten minutes on a towel is enough to hold onto most of what you've built.

topic: Leg pain when walking that eases when you sit (spinal stenosis)

slides.headline: Legs ache walking, ease when you sit?
slides.sub: One common reason, and why walking often still helps.

slides.title: One common pattern
slides.body: Aching, heaviness or tingling in the buttocks or legs that builds as you walk and eases when you sit or lean forward is often linked to narrowing around the nerves in the lower back.

slides.title: Why leaning forward helps
slides.body: Bending forward opens the space around the nerves a little. That's why leaning on a shopping trolley or sitting down often brings relief within a few minutes.

slides.title: Walking is still worthwhile
slides.body: Walking in shorter bouts with rest breaks, or cycling on a stationary bike, keeps you fit without pushing through big symptoms. Many people gradually build their distance this way.

slides.title: Strength and flexibility help
slides.body: Current guidelines suggest exercise as a first step. Building hip and leg strength, trunk control and gentle forward-bending stretches can make daily walking and standing more comfortable over time.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: See a doctor promptly for numbness around the groin, changes in bladder or bowel control, or weakness that is getting worse. Leg pain from poor circulation can feel similar, so get it assessed.

topic: Back pain when bending to put on shoes and socks

slides.headline: Socks and shoes the hardest part?
slides.sub: Why bending forward can hurt, and some easier ways to get dressed.

slides.title: Why this movement catches
slides.body: Pulling on socks means bending forward, balancing and reaching all at once. When your back is irritable, that combination often feels worse than bending to pick something up.

slides.title: Sit down to dress
slides.body: Sit on the edge of the bed or a chair, then bring your foot up onto the opposite knee. This keeps your back more upright and takes the balance challenge away.

slides.title: Use the tools
slides.body: A long-handled shoehorn and slip-on shoes make flare-up days easier. Needing them for a while isn't a step backwards, it's a sensible way to keep moving.

slides.title: Train the movement back
slides.body: Gentle hip hinges, seated forward bends and knee-to-chest stretches, done little and often, usually help the movement feel easier. Most people improve as confidence and mobility return.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain that spreads below the knee, numbness or weakness in the leg, or pain that is worsening instead of settling is worth an assessment before you push through.

topic: Staying active over the Christmas break

slides.headline: Five ways to keep moving this break
slides.sub: Holidays change your routine. Your body still likes regular movement.

slides.title: 1. Keep one anchor habit
slides.body: Pick one thing you'll do most days, like a morning walk or ten minutes of exercises. One small habit is easier to keep than a full routine when every day looks different.

slides.title: 2. Swap, don't stop
slides.body: Gym closed or away from home? Swap in a beach walk, a swim, a bike ride or a bodyweight session. Your tissues care about regular load more than where it comes from.

slides.title: 3. Move between long sits
slides.body: Long drives, flights and marathon lunches add up. Get up every 30 to 60 minutes where you can. A lap of the backyard or a stretch at a rest stop counts.

slides.title: 4. Go easy on the new stuff
slides.body: Holidays bring new activities: cricket on the beach, long hikes, paddleboarding. Start with a shorter version and build up. Sore the next day is common, so plan an easier day after.

slides.title: 5. Beat the heat
slides.body: Move early or late in the day, carry water and wear a hat. In very hot weather, shorter or indoor sessions are a sensible swap.

topic: Getting up off the floor: a skill worth practising

slides.headline: Can you get up off the floor easily?
slides.sub: It's a skill, and like any skill it improves with practice.

slides.title: Why it matters
slides.body: Playing with grandkids, stretching on a mat, or getting up after a slip all need this skill. Practising it builds leg strength, balance and the confidence to get down there at all.

slides.title: Break it into steps
slides.body: From lying, roll to your side, push up onto hands and knees, bring one foot forward into a half kneel, then push up through that leg. Use a chair or couch for support to start.

slides.title: Practise both ways
slides.body: Get down the same way in reverse. Most people have a stronger side, so practise leading with each leg. Three to five times a day is a good starting point.

slides.title: Build the strength behind it
slides.body: Sit-to-stands from a chair, step-ups and lunges holding a bench all make floor transfers easier. Over a few weeks, try using less help from your hands.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: If you've had a fall, feel dizzy when you stand, or have knee, hip or back pain that stops you practising, get it assessed. A physio can adapt the steps for you.

slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios can assess your strength and balance and set up a floor practice routine that suits you. Book online via the link in bio.

slides.headline: Stiff, achy hands in the morning?
slides.sub: Hand osteoarthritis is common. Movement and strength usually help.

slides.title: What's going on
slides.body: Osteoarthritis in the hands often affects the finger joints and the base of the thumb. Stiffness in the morning, aching after use and knobbly joints are common. It varies a lot between people.

slides.title: Move them every day
slides.body: Gentle range exercises help: make a loose fist, then spread your fingers wide. Touch your thumb to each fingertip. Ten slow reps, a few times a day, often ease stiffness.

slides.title: Warm up first
slides.body: Many people find their hands move more easily after warmth. Try the exercises after a warm shower, or with your hands resting in a bowl of warm water for a few minutes first.

slides.title: Strength is part of it
slides.body: Squeezing a soft ball, pinching putty and lifting light objects build grip strength. Stronger muscles can help support the joints through daily tasks like opening jars.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Sudden swelling, redness and heat in a joint, a joint that's changing shape quickly, or pain that stops you doing daily tasks are worth getting assessed by your GP or physio.

slides.headline: Off a long-haul flight and stiff all over?
slides.sub: Where massage fits after a long trip, and what else helps.

slides.title: Why flights leave you stiff
slides.body: Many hours in a cramped seat, little movement and disrupted sleep often leave necks, backs and legs feeling tight. It's usually stiffness from staying still, not injury.

slides.title: Move first, massage next
slides.body: A walk in daylight the day you land and some gentle stretching usually help most. A massage a day or two later can add to that by easing tight, sore areas.

slides.title: What a session can target
slides.body: Common areas after a flight are the neck and upper back from sleeping upright, the lower back, and the calves. Your therapist can adjust pressure to how you feel.

slides.title: Go gentler after travel
slides.body: Tired and dehydrated bodies can feel more tender. A moderate session is often a better choice than deep work. Drink water and plan an easy day afterwards.

slides.title: When to see a doctor
slides.body: Calf pain, swelling, warmth or redness in one leg, or chest pain or breathlessness after a flight needs a doctor promptly, not a massage. Call 000 in an emergency.

topic: Neck pain when driving: mirrors, headrest and breaks

slides.headline: Neck stiff after every road trip?
slides.sub: Your mirrors, headrest and breaks matter more than you might think.

slides.title: Set your seat first
slides.body: Sit with hips back in the seat and the backrest slightly reclined. Your hands should rest on the wheel with elbows gently bent, so your shoulders aren't reaching.

slides.title: Mirrors as a posture cue
slides.body: Adjust your mirrors while sitting tall. If you start slumping, the mirrors will look off. That's a useful reminder to sit back up, rather than readjusting them.

slides.title: Bring the headrest up
slides.body: The middle of the headrest should sit roughly level with the back of your head, and close to it. It's there to protect your neck, and it gives you something to rest back against.

slides.title: Break every two hours
slides.body: Stop, get out and walk for a few minutes. Look over each shoulder, roll your shoulders and do a few chin tucks. Share the driving where you can.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain spreading down an arm, pins and needles or weakness in the hand, headaches that keep building, or neck pain after a car accident are worth an assessment.

topic: Menopause and joint aches: staying strong

slides.headline: Menopause and new joint aches?
slides.sub: It's common. Strength training is one of the most useful tools.

slides.title: A common experience
slides.body: Many women notice more joint aches and stiffness around menopause. Hormone changes can affect muscles, tendons and joints. Aches often show up in the hands, shoulders, hips and knees.

slides.title: Strength is your friend
slides.body: Research suggests regular strength training helps maintain muscle and bone, which both tend to decline at this stage. Two to three sessions a week is a good target.

slides.title: Start where you are
slides.body: You don't need heavy weights on day one. Squats to a chair, step-ups, wall push-ups and rows with a band are a solid base. Build the load gradually over weeks.

slides.title: Keep the rest of the mix
slides.body: Walking, swimming or cycling, good sleep and staying social all help. Some soreness when starting is normal. Aim for effort that feels challenging but manageable.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A hot, swollen joint, pain after a fall, pain that wakes you every night, or aches with fever or feeling unwell need your GP. Talk to your GP about menopause care too.

topic: Coming back after a holiday break: ease in

slides.headline: Back to training after the break?
slides.sub: Two weeks off? Ease in so the first week doesn't set you back.

slides.title: You've lost less than you think
slides.body: A couple of weeks off usually costs very little strength or fitness. What changes is how your tissues tolerate load, so the first sessions back can feel harder than expected.

slides.title: Start at about half
slides.body: For the first week, try roughly half your usual volume: fewer sets, shorter runs or lighter weights. Then build up over two to three weeks if you pull up well.

slides.title: Use the next-morning test
slides.body: Mild soreness that eases within a day or two is normal. Soreness that's worse the next morning, or lasts longer, is a sign to hold at that level before adding more.

slides.title: Mind the resolution rush
slides.body: New year motivation is great, but adding extra sessions and intensity in the same week is a common cause of niggles. Change one thing at a time.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain that changes how you move, swelling, pain that builds during a session, or a niggle that keeps coming back is worth an assessment before you push on.

topic: Back pain in adult fast bowlers

slides.headline: Fast bowler with a sore back?
slides.sub: Adult quicks load their backs hard. Here's how to manage it.

slides.title: Why fast bowling loads the back
slides.body: Bowling combines bending, side bending and twisting at speed, with big forces through the front leg on landing. Repeated overs add up, especially early in the season.

slides.title: Watch your overs
slides.body: Sudden jumps in bowling load are a common trigger. Build your overs gradually across the pre-season and track how many you bowl in training and games each week.

slides.title: Strength off the pitch
slides.body: Trunk strength, hip and glute strength and single-leg control help your body handle the load. Two short gym sessions a week can make a real difference over a season.

slides.title: Action matters too
slides.body: Some actions put more twist through the lower back. A coach and physio can look at your run-up, delivery stride and landing together without rebuilding your whole action.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Back pain that's worse when you arch or twist, pain that lingers after bowling, leg pain or numbness, or pain at night is worth an assessment before your next spell.

slides.headline: Keep bowling through summer
slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios assess your back, strength and bowling load, then build a plan for the season. Book online via the link in bio.

topic: Thongs vs supportive shoes for summer walking

slides.headline: Thongs all summer: good or bad?
slides.sub: Thongs aren't the enemy. It depends on how far and where you walk.

slides.title: Thongs are fine for short trips
slides.body: Beach, pool, a quick walk to the shops: thongs are usually fine. Most feet cope well with short stretches of low support, and going barefoot at times has its place too.

slides.title: Why long walks feel different
slides.body: To keep a thong on, your toes grip with every step. Over long distances, that can tire the feet and calves and irritate the heel or front of the foot.

slides.title: Pick your footwear for the job
slides.body: For long walks, uneven paths or lots of standing, a shoe or sandal with a heel strap and some cushioning is usually more comfortable. Supportive thongs with arch contouring are another option.

slides.title: Build up gradually
slides.body: Went from runners all year to thongs all summer? Heel and arch pain often follow a sudden change. Mix up your footwear and increase thong time gradually.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Heel pain with the first steps in the morning, a sore spot on the top of the foot, swelling or pain that's getting worse is worth an assessment.

slides.headline: Feet sore this summer?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios assess your feet, footwear and walking and help you choose what suits you. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:

For long walks, uneven paths or lots of standing, try a sandal with a heel strap or a cushioned shoe, and build up thong time gradually. Heel pain first thing in the morning or a sore spot on the top of your foot is worth getting checked.

topic: Setting a movement goal for the new year

slides.headline: New year, one movement goal
slides.sub: Skip the big resolution. Here's how to set one you'll keep.

slides.title: Make it specific
slides.body: 'Get fit' is hard to act on. 'Walk 30 minutes before work on weekdays' or 'two strength sessions a week' tells you exactly what to do and when you've done it.

slides.title: Link it to something you care about
slides.body: Goals stick better with a reason behind them: keeping up with the kids, hiking a favourite track, or carrying the shopping in one trip. Write that reason down.

slides.title: Start smaller than you think
slides.body: Pick a starting level you could do on a busy week. Once it feels routine, add a little. Most people do better with small, steady steps than a big start.

slides.title: Plan for the tricky weeks
slides.body: Travel, work deadlines and sick kids happen. Decide ahead what your minimum version looks like, like ten minutes instead of forty, so the habit survives.

slides.title: Check in every month
slides.body: Take a minute at the end of each month to review. What went well? What got in the way? Adjust the goal rather than giving up on it.

slides.headline: Want help setting your goal?
slides.body: Our team can help you set a realistic goal and plan the steps, whatever your starting point. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:
Skip the giant resolution this year. One clear movement goal goes further. ✨

Specific beats vague: 'two strength sessions a week' is easier to act on than 'get fit'. Link it to something you care about, like keeping up with the kids or hiking a favourite track.

Start smaller than you think, decide what your minimum version looks like for busy weeks, and check in at the end of each month to adjust. Small, steady steps usually beat a big start that fades by February.

topic: Jumping and landing: training your knees for sport

slides.headline: How do your knees handle landing?
slides.sub: Jumping and landing are trainable skills. Here's where to start.

slides.title: Landing is where load peaks
slides.body: In netball, basketball, volleyball and touch, landings and sudden stops put big forces through the knee. Good control spreads that load across your hips, knees and ankles.

slides.title: Land soft and quiet
slides.body: Land on the balls of your feet and let your ankles, knees and hips bend together. Aim for a quiet landing, with knees tracking in line with your toes.

slides.title: Start with two feet
slides.body: Practise small jumps onto and off a low step, sticking each landing for two seconds. Once that feels controlled, add height, then single-leg hops, then direction changes.

slides.title: Strength underpins it all
slides.body: Squats, lunges, step-downs and calf raises build the capacity to absorb landings. Research suggests warm-up programs with strength and landing drills can reduce knee injuries in sport.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A pop with swelling, your knee giving way, locking, or pain below or around the kneecap that builds with jumping is worth an assessment before you keep playing.

slides.headline: Train your landings
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios assess how you jump and land and build a program for your sport. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:
How do your knees handle landing? It's a skill you can train.

Jumping and landing put some of the biggest loads through your knees in sport, especially in netball, basketball, volleyball and touch. Good control spreads that load across your hips, knees and ankles.

Start by landing soft and quiet with knees in line with toes. Practise small two-foot jumps and stick each landing, then progress to single-leg hops and direction changes. Squats, lunges and step-downs build the strength behind it. A pop, swelling or knee giving way needs an assessment.

topic: Wrist pain after a fall on an outstretched hand

slides.headline: Fell on your hand? Check the wrist
slides.sub: Most wrist sprains settle, but some injuries need a closer look.

slides.title: A common way to get hurt
slides.body: Slipping on a wet deck, falling off a bike or a scooter, or tripping at the beach: we instinctively put a hand out. That can strain ligaments or injure a bone in the wrist.

slides.title: First few days
slides.body: Protect it, keep it raised and use a cold pack for short periods. Remove rings early in case of swelling. Keep your fingers, elbow and shoulder moving gently.

slides.title: Get it checked if bone is possible
slides.body: Tenderness in the hollow at the base of the thumb, swelling, a change in shape or trouble gripping can point to a fracture. These often need an X-ray through your GP or emergency department.

slides.title: Rebuilding movement and grip
slides.body: Once serious injury is ruled out, gentle range exercises, then grip and weight-bearing work, help most wrists recover. Pushing up from a chair is a useful later test.

slides.title: If it's slow to settle
slides.body: Some wrist injuries don't show much at first. If pain in the wrist hasn't eased after a week or two, an assessment is a sensible next step.

slides.headline: Wrist still sore after a fall?
slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios assess your wrist, arrange next steps with your GP if needed, and guide your rehab. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:
Fell on an outstretched hand and your wrist is still sore?

Putting a hand out when you fall is instinctive. Summer slips on wet decks, bike and scooter spills all do it. Many cases are sprains that settle, but some involve a small bone at the base of the thumb that can be easy to miss.

Tenderness in the hollow at the base of the thumb, swelling, a change in shape or trouble gripping are worth getting checked, often with an X-ray through your GP or emergency department. Once that's ruled out, rehab rebuilds movement and grip.
